item.research_question: How do different powder metallurgy processing routes (CIP, sintering, HIP, swaging, SPS, HPT) affect the microstructure, oxygen content, porosity, and mechanical properties of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Three initial powder types were used: (1) Elemental powders mixed for 10 h at 45 rpm and cold isostatically pressed (CIP) at 400 MPa; (2) Mechanical alloying (MA) via high energy ball milling for 42 h; (3) Gas atomized (AT) powder. Subsequent routes included sintering at 1400 °C for 16 h, HIP at 1400 °C/190 MPa for 2 h, hot swaging at 950 °C (with and without Ti-alloy envelope), Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1300 °C/80 MPa for 2 min, and High Pressure Torsion (HPT) at 2.5 GPa for 15 revolutions.
item.test_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with 98.1 N load; microstructure analyzed via LM, SEM (BSE), and XRD; oxygen content determined by gas fusion; porosity via SEM image analysis; dislocation density via positron lifetime spectroscopy.
key_findings: The AT-SPS-HPT specimen achieved the lowest oxygen content (0.12 ± 0.02 wt %) and was the only sample with a single-phase bcc random solid solution and zero porosity.
HPT deformation of the AT-SPS specimen refined the grain size from ~50 μm to below 0.5 μm (500 nm) while maintaining a single bcc phase.
The AT-SPS-HPT specimen exhibited a hardness of 410 ± 5 HV10, whereas the MA-SPS-HPT specimen reached 680 ± 5 HV10 due to higher oxygen content and oxide precipitation.
Hot swaging at 950 °C failed to produce a fully dense specimen due to cracking, even when the sample was enveloped in a titanium alloy.
Oxygen content increased significantly during processing: from 0.55 wt % in green compacts to 0.84 wt % in HIP-treated samples and 1.07 wt % in mechanically alloyed samples.
Dislocation density in AT-SPS-HPT and MA-SPS-HPT samples exceeded 5 × 10^14 m^-2, confirmed by positron lifetime spectroscopy showing saturated trapping.
Samples with oxygen content above 0.8 wt % showed a sharp increase in hardness, attributed to the formation of HfO2 precipitates.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that high oxygen content causes embrittlement and prevents the formation of a single-phase random solid solution by stabilizing secondary phases like HfO2 and hcp phases. The single-phase bcc structure in AT-SPS is attributed to the high cooling rate (~300 °C/min) during SPS, which suppresses phase separation. Grain refinement and hardness increase in HPT samples are caused by severe plastic deformation generating high dislocation densities, while the extreme hardness in MA-SPS-HPT is additionally driven by oxygen solid solution strengthening and oxide particle precipitation.
item.limitations: The authors state that hot swaging resulted in specimen cracking, preventing full densification. The MA-SPS-HPT specimen was damaged and separated into pieces during HPT, making its results disputable. The low hardness of HEAP-HIP samples is attributed to incomplete dissolution of Ta/Nb particles and residual porosity, with the cause of the hardness difference remaining unclear.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the possibility of hot deformation for alloys with increased oxygen content cannot be excluded under suitable conditions (e.g., low strain rate or higher processing temperature) but requires more detailed study.
quotes: The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content.

The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 500 nm.
The oxygen content in the initial powder used for sintering (HEAP sample) was relatively high (~0.55 wt %), as seen in Table 2. However, it could be seen that it increased during further processing.
